skills.name: Laws of exponents
skills.intro_md: When you multiply powers with the same base you add the exponents; when you divide them you subtract; when a power is raised to a power you multiply.
misconceptions: Multiplying the exponents when multiplying powers
Applying the exponent to the coefficient only

skills.name: Scientific notation
skills.intro_md: Scientific notation writes a number as a value between 1 and 10 times a power of ten. A positive exponent means a big number, a negative exponent means a small one.
misconceptions: Keeping the decimal in the wrong place (the first factor must be 1 to 10)
Sign error when moving the decimal to the right

skills.name: Simplifying linear expressions
skills.intro_md: Combine like terms by adding their coefficients, and use the distributive property to remove brackets before combining.
misconceptions: Distributing to the first term only
Dropping the sign in front of a subtracted bracket

skills.name: Equations with variables on both sides
skills.intro_md: Move every variable term to one side and every constant to the other, then divide by the coefficient. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other.
misconceptions: Moving a term without changing its sign
Dividing only one side by the coefficient

skills.name: Solving systems by substitution
skills.intro_md: When one equation already gives you y (or x) in terms of the other variable, replace that variable in the second equation. You get one equation with one unknown.
misconceptions: Substituting into the same equation instead of the other one
Stopping after finding one variable and forgetting the other

skills.name: The Pythagorean theorem
skills.intro_md: In a right triangle the two legs satisfy a² + b² = c², where c is always the side across from the right angle (the longest side).
misconceptions: Putting a leg where the hypotenuse belongs
Adding the squares instead of subtracting to find a missing leg

skills.name: Solving one-variable equations
skills.intro_md: Undo operations in reverse order: first the addition or subtraction, then the multiplication or division, working towards x on its own.
misconceptions: Dividing before undoing the constant
Losing the negative sign when dividing

skills.name: Linear equations with variables on both sides
skills.intro_md: Collect the variable terms on one side and the numbers on the other. If brackets are involved, distribute first.
misconceptions: Distributing to only one term in the bracket
Sign errors when a bracket is subtracted

skills.name: Linear inequalities
skills.intro_md: Solve inequalities like equations, with one exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number flips the inequality sign.
misconceptions: Forgetting to flip the sign when dividing by a negative
Treating 'at most' as a strict inequality

skills.name: Slope and intercepts
skills.intro_md: Slope is rise over run: (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁). In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.
misconceptions: Putting the change in x on top
Reading the intercept as a point instead of the y-value

skills.name: Systems of equations by substitution
skills.intro_md: Solve one equation for a variable, substitute it into the other, solve, then back-substitute to find the second variable.
misconceptions: Substituting back into the rearranged equation
Reporting only one of the two values

skills.name: Factoring quadratics
skills.intro_md: For x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Those become the two constants in the factored form.
misconceptions: Choosing numbers that multiply to b instead of c
Losing a sign when c is negative

skills.name: One-dimensional kinematics
skills.intro_md: The four constant-acceleration equations connect v, v₀, a, t and Δx. Pick the one that contains what you know and what you need.
misconceptions: Using a constant-acceleration equation when the acceleration changes
Sign errors from mixing up v and v₀

skills.name: Newton's second law
skills.intro_md: ΣF = ma uses the net force, not one force. Draw the free-body diagram first, then add the components along the direction of motion.
misconceptions: Using the applied force instead of the net force
Forgetting that the normal force is not always mg

skills.name: Work done by a constant force
skills.intro_md: W = F d cos θ uses the component of the force along the displacement. A force perpendicular to the motion does no work.
misconceptions: Ignoring the angle and using F·d
Counting friction as positive work

skills.name: Work done by a varying force
skills.intro_md: When the force changes, work is the area under the force-versus-position graph, not force times distance.
misconceptions: Using the final force for the whole distance
Treating a triangular area as a rectangle

skills.name: The work-energy theorem
skills.intro_md: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK. It is often easier than tracking forces through time.
misconceptions: Using only one force's work for W_net
Forgetting that friction does negative work

skills.name: Momentum and impulse in one dimension
skills.intro_md: p = mv, and impulse J = FΔt equals the change in momentum. In a collision with no external force, total momentum is conserved.
misconceptions: Forgetting that momentum is a vector
Using kinetic energy conservation for every collision

skills.name: Linear equations and systems
skills.intro_md: SAT linear questions reward translating words into equations and solving systems efficiently rather than elegantly.
misconceptions: Solving for x when the question asks for an expression
One solution when the system has two unknowns

skills.name: Percent change and percent of
skills.intro_md: Percent change is (new − old) / old × 100. A percent decrease multiplies by (1 − rate); a percent increase multiplies by (1 + rate).
misconceptions: Dividing by the new value instead of the original
Adding successive percentages instead of multiplying the factors

skills.name: Ratios, rates and proportions
skills.intro_md: Set up a proportion with matching units, then cross-multiply. For part-to-whole ratios, the total is the sum of the parts.
misconceptions: Mixing units in the two sides of a proportion
Treating a part-to-part ratio as part-to-whole

skills.name: Area and perimeter
skills.intro_md: Know the rectangle, triangle and circle formulas cold, and split composite shapes into pieces you can measure.
misconceptions: Using the diameter instead of the radius
Forgetting to halve for a triangle's area

skills.name: Function notation and composition
skills.intro_md: f(3) means substitute 3 for x. f(g(2)) means evaluate g(2) first, then put that result into f.
misconceptions: Multiplying f by the input instead of substituting
Evaluating the outer function first in a composition

skills.name: Cell structure and function
skills.intro_md: Each organelle does one job well: mitochondria make ATP, the rough ER builds proteins for export, and the cell wall lets a plant cell take on water without bursting.
misconceptions: Treating the ribosome as the cell's energy source
Forgetting that a plant cell has both a membrane and a wall

skills.name: Bonding and the mole
skills.intro_md: Moles are just a count: moles = mass ÷ molar mass, and one mole always holds 6.0 × 10²³ particles. Ionic bonds transfer electrons; covalent bonds share them.
misconceptions: Multiplying mass by molar mass instead of dividing
Confusing the number of molecules with the number of atoms

skills.name: Everyday science concepts
skills.intro_md: Everyday science asks you to reason from what you already know: what things are made of, which changes create a new substance, and how the world behaves.
misconceptions: Calling a mixture a chemical change
Judging hardness from how an object looks instead of from a scratch test

skills.name: Commas and sentence boundaries
skills.intro_md: Two complete sentences cannot be joined by a comma alone. Use a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction — and use a semicolon, never a comma, before a conjunctive adverb like 'however'.
misconceptions: Joining two complete sentences with only a comma
Putting a semicolon before a coordinating conjunction

skills.name: Inference in a short passage
skills.intro_md: An inference is the smallest conclusion the details support. Name the detail that changed, then ask what that change would cause.
misconceptions: Choosing a statement the passage never implies
Confusing what happened with why it happened

skills.name: Words in context
skills.intro_md: Cover the blank and predict your own word from the sentence's logic, especially contrast words like 'although' and 'rather than'. Then pick the choice closest to it.
misconceptions: Picking a word that sounds impressive but ignores the contrast
Using a familiar meaning that does not fit this sentence

skills.name: Sentence boundaries on the SAT
skills.intro_md: Most boundary questions come down to one test: could each side of the punctuation stand alone as a sentence? If both can, you need a semicolon or a period.
misconceptions: Choosing a colon after a fragment
Splitting a subject from its verb with a semicolon

skills.name: Rates and percents
skills.intro_md: Find the unit rate first, then scale. Successive percent discounts multiply (0.75 × 0.90), they never add to a single 35% cut.
misconceptions: Adding successive percentages instead of multiplying factors
Dividing distance by the wrong time

skills.name: ACT science: reading data
skills.intro_md: ACT science rarely asks for outside knowledge. Read the axes and table headers, find the trend, then answer exactly what the question asks about that trend.
misconceptions: Reading a data table as if the rows were time order when the header says otherwise
Answering from general science knowledge instead of the figure

skills.name: Usage and punctuation
skills.intro_md: Find the real subject before choosing the verb form — words like 'each', 'every' and 'the team' are singular even when they are followed by a plural noun.
misconceptions: Matching the verb to the nearest noun instead of the subject
Putting the apostrophe in the wrong place for a plural possessive

skills.name: Casework and counting
skills.intro_md: Counting is organisation: multiply independent choices, divide out repeats, and count paths by choosing which steps are the horizontal ones.
misconceptions: Forgetting to divide by repeated letters
Adding counts for overlapping sets instead of subtracting the overlap

skills.name: Divisibility and primes
skills.intro_md: Prime factorisation answers divisor-count and remainder questions. For factorials, count each prime's multiples, then its squares, then its cubes.
misconceptions: Counting divisors without adding one to each exponent
Missing the 9s and 27s when counting powers in a factorial

skills.name: Multi-step word problems
skills.intro_md: Word problems are a chain of small steps. Name what each sentence asks you to compute, keep the units with the numbers, and only then do the arithmetic.
misconceptions: Answering with the last number computed instead of the quantity requested
Mixing units such as minutes and hours in the same product

skills.name: AMC 8 geometry
skills.intro_md: Most AMC 8 geometry is one formula plus one right triangle: know the Pythagorean triples, the triangle area formula and 2πr.
misconceptions: Using the diameter as the radius
Forgetting the ½ in the triangle area formula

skills.name: AMC 8 counting and logic
skills.intro_md: Organise by cases or by size. Count small squares before big ones, and remove double counting whenever two lists overlap.
misconceptions: Counting only unit squares in a grid question
Forgetting to subtract the overlap in 'divisible by 3 or 5' problems

skills.name: AMC 10 algebra
skills.intro_md: Work with the expression the question asks about rather than solving for x. Squaring a sum like x + 1/x, and Vieta's sum −b/a, do most of the work.
misconceptions: Squaring a sum without the cross term
Using b instead of −b/a for the sum of roots

skills.name: AMC 10 geometry
skills.intro_md: Drop a perpendicular: a chord of a circle becomes a right triangle with half the chord as one leg. Split regular hexagons into six equilateral triangles.
misconceptions: Using half the chord as the distance to the centre
Using the side length as the height of an equilateral triangle

skills.name: AMC 12 functions and trig
skills.intro_md: Function questions are about structure: sin(kx) has period 2π/k, a quadratic's minimum sits at its vertex, and an inverse undoes the original equation.
misconceptions: Reading f⁻¹(7) as f(7)
Multiplying the period by k instead of dividing

skills.name: AMC 12 combinatorics
skills.intro_md: Choose whether order matters before you compute anything, and use 'at least one' = 'all' − 'none' when the direct count is messy.
misconceptions: Using permutations when only the group matters
Counting each handshake twice

skills.name: Place value and rounding
skills.intro_md: Every digit has a value set by its place: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. Round by looking at the digit to the right of the place you are keeping.
misconceptions: Reading a digit as its face value instead of its place value
Rounding up when the next digit is 4 or less

skills.name: Multiplication and division
skills.intro_md: Multiplication is repeated equal groups; division asks how many groups fit. Arrays and area models show both at once.
misconceptions: Adding the groups instead of multiplying
Mixing up the divisor with the quotient

skills.name: Fractions and how to compare them
skills.intro_md: A fraction is a number of equal parts of a whole. Multiply top and bottom by the same number to rename it, and compare fractions over a common denominator.
misconceptions: Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction
Adding numerators and denominators separately

skills.name: Decimals and percent
skills.intro_md: Percent means out of 100, so 35% is 0.35. Percent change is the change divided by the original amount, not by the new one.
misconceptions: Subtracting a percent as if it were a dollar amount
Dividing the change by the new price

skills.name: Ratios, rates and proportion
skills.intro_md: A ratio compares two amounts; a rate compares amounts with different units. Find the unit rate, then scale it to the quantity you need.
misconceptions: Adding the same amount to both parts of a ratio
Using the wrong base when scaling

skills.name: Area, perimeter and volume
skills.intro_md: Perimeter is distance around, area is space covered (length × width, half for a triangle, πr² for a circle) and volume is space inside a solid.
misconceptions: Using base × height for a triangle without halving
Confusing area with perimeter

skills.name: Quadratics
skills.intro_md: Factor first, then use vertex form (x − h)² + k for the turning point. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you how many real roots exist.
misconceptions: Reading the vertex sign from (x − h)² the wrong way
Forgetting the quadratic has two roots

skills.name: Functions, composition and inverses
skills.intro_md: A function maps inputs to outputs. Compose inside-out, and remember that changes inside the brackets shift horizontally while changes outside shift vertically.
misconceptions: Composing in the wrong order (g(f(x)) instead of f(g(x)))
Shifting left/right when the change is outside the function

skills.name: Exponents and logarithms
skills.intro_md: A logarithm answers 'what exponent gives this number?'. Adding logs multiplies their arguments; subtracting logs divides them.
misconceptions: Thinking log(a + b) = log a + log b
Multiplying logs instead of adding them

skills.name: Sequences and series
skills.intro_md: Arithmetic sequences add a constant difference; geometric sequences multiply by a constant ratio. An infinite geometric series converges only when |r| < 1.
misconceptions: Treating a geometric sequence as arithmetic
Forgetting the a in a/(1 − r)

skills.name: Trigonometry
skills.intro_md: SOH-CAH-TOA for right triangles, and the unit circle for every angle. The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 links the two.
misconceptions: Swapping sine and cosine ratios
Using degrees when radians are required

skills.name: Vectors
skills.intro_md: A vector has size and direction. Add component by component, take the length with Pythagoras, and use the dot product to test perpendicularity.
misconceptions: Adding lengths instead of components
Confusing the dot product with multiplication

skills.name: Limits and continuity
skills.intro_md: A limit is where the function is heading, not where it lands. Factor or divide by the dominant power when direct substitution gives 0/0 or ∞/∞.
misconceptions: Reading 0/0 as zero
Assuming a limit exists when the two sides disagree

skills.name: Derivative rules
skills.intro_md: The power rule brings the exponent down; the product, quotient and chain rules cover combined functions. A derivative is a rate of change.
misconceptions: Differentiating a product as the product of derivatives
Forgetting the inner derivative in the chain rule

skills.name: Optimisation and related rates
skills.intro_md: Set the derivative to zero to find candidates, then check the endpoints and the second derivative. In related-rates problems, differentiate the relationship with respect to time.
misconceptions: Checking only f′ = 0 and ignoring endpoints
Differentiating a related-rates equation with respect to the wrong variable

skills.name: Integrals and the fundamental theorem
skills.intro_md: An integral accumulates area. Add one to the exponent and divide by the new exponent, then evaluate the antiderivative at the limits.
misconceptions: Forgetting +C on an indefinite integral
Substituting limits before finding the antiderivative

skills.name: Sequences and series (BC)
skills.intro_md: Use the ratio test for a radius of convergence. Geometric series sum to a/(1 − r), and the harmonic series is the classic divergent case.
misconceptions: Assuming terms going to zero makes a series converge
Summing a geometric series without checking |r| < 1

skills.name: Describing data
skills.intro_md: Centre (mean, median) and spread (range, standard deviation) describe a data set. Outliers move the mean far more than the median.
misconceptions: Confusing the median with the mean
Thinking standard deviation is a centre

skills.name: Probability and independence
skills.intro_md: Multiply probabilities for independent events, and never forget the denominator drops when you draw without replacement.
misconceptions: Adding probabilities for 'and' events
Forgetting that without replacement changes the total

skills.name: AIME number theory
skills.intro_md: Prime factorise first: divisor counts and gcds fall out of the exponents. Modular arithmetic solves repeated-power remainders.
misconceptions: Counting divisors without the (a + 1)(b + 1) rule
Adding counts in an inclusion-exclusion problem without subtracting the overlap

skills.name: AIME combinatorics
skills.intro_md: Decide whether order matters before writing anything. Round tables divide out the rotations; paths on a grid are a choice of steps.
misconceptions: Using permutations when only the set matters
Forgetting to divide out rotational symmetry

skills.name: AIME geometry
skills.intro_md: Look for a right triangle you can use: 5-12-13, 6-8-10, tangents perpendicular to radii. Area formulas often beat coordinate work.
misconceptions: Using the hypotenuse as a leg
Forgetting that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius

skills.name: USAMO algebra
skills.intro_md: Symmetric expressions can be rewritten in terms of sums and products. Squaring an equation usually brings a helpful cross term.
misconceptions: Squaring a sum and ignoring the 2ab term
Forgetting that a factored product is prime only when one factor is 1

skills.name: USAMO number theory
skills.intro_md: Count factors of 5 for trailing zeros, factor n² − 1 into consecutive numbers, and check parity before anything else.
misconceptions: Counting factors of 2 instead of 5 for trailing zeros
Assuming n² − 1 is never divisible by 8

skills.name: IMO geometry
skills.intro_md: Circle theorems do most of the work: opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, and tangents meet radii at right angles.
misconceptions: Treating every cyclic quadrilateral as a rectangle
Confusing interior and exterior angle sums

skills.name: IMO inequalities
skills.intro_md: AM-GM is the first tool: for positive numbers the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean, with equality when the numbers are equal.
misconceptions: Applying AM-GM to numbers that are not positive
Assuming equality can happen with unequal numbers

skills.name: MATHCOUNTS sprint round
skills.intro_md: The sprint round rewards clean arithmetic under time: unit rates, percent change and counting digits are all one-step ideas if you set them up right.
misconceptions: Adding percentages instead of applying them to a base
Counting a digit twice in a 'contains' question

skills.name: MATHCOUNTS target round
skills.intro_md: Target problems take two or three steps: factor, count with care, then check the last digit or the end of the number.
misconceptions: Using 5 choices per digit when only odd digits are allowed
Counting trailing zeros from multiples of 10 only

skills.name: AMC 8 geometry
skills.intro_md: AMC 8 geometry is mostly formulas used exactly once: Pythagoras, perimeter, angle sums, circumference.
misconceptions: Adding sides instead of squaring them for a diagonal
Using the radius where the diameter is given

skills.name: AMC 10 counting
skills.intro_md: Choose between combinations and permutations by asking whether order matters, and count half of a symmetric set when the question asks for even numbers or sums.
misconceptions: Counting orderings when only the group matters
Forgetting that a subset can be empty

skills.name: AMC 12 trigonometry
skills.intro_md: Use the unit-circle values, the double-angle identities and the period 2π/k for sin(kx). Quadrant signs decide whether an answer is positive.
misconceptions: Ignoring the quadrant sign
Using 2π as the period regardless of the coefficient

skills.name: Living things
skills.intro_md: Living things grow, reproduce and use energy. Plants make food by photosynthesis; fungi decompose; animals are consumers.
misconceptions: Thinking anything that moves is alive
Believing fungi are plants

skills.name: Matter and changes
skills.intro_md: Matter is solid, liquid or gas. A physical change keeps the same substance; a chemical change makes a new one.
misconceptions: Mixing up the Celsius and Fahrenheit freezing points
Calling dissolving a chemical change

skills.name: Forces and motion
skills.intro_md: A force changes motion. Weight is the pull of gravity (mass × g), and Newton's third law pairs equal, opposite forces.
misconceptions: Confusing mass with weight
Thinking a moving object needs a constant force

skills.name: Earth and space
skills.intro_md: Earth spins for day and night and orbits the Sun for the year. The tilted axis gives the seasons; the Moon's phases cycle about every 29.5 days.
misconceptions: Explaining seasons with distance from the Sun
Thinking the Moon makes its own light

skills.name: Energy
skills.intro_md: Energy is stored (potential, chemical) or moving (kinetic). It is transferred and transformed, never created or destroyed.
misconceptions: Thinking energy disappears when something stops
Confusing energy with force

skills.name: Waves and sound
skills.intro_md: Waves carry energy without carrying matter. Sound needs a medium, and higher frequency means higher pitch.
misconceptions: Thinking sound can travel through a vacuum
Confusing volume with pitch

skills.name: Statics and equilibrium
skills.intro_md: A body in equilibrium has zero net force and zero net moment. Moments are force times perpendicular distance.
misconceptions: Checking forces but forgetting moments
Using the total load as one support reaction

skills.name: Circuits and Ohm's law
skills.intro_md: V = IR relates voltage, current and resistance. Series resistances add; parallel ones combine reciprocally. Power is I²R.
misconceptions: Adding parallel resistances directly
Using V = IR as the power formula

skills.name: Thermodynamics
skills.intro_md: Energy is conserved and entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Carnot efficiency is 1 − T_cold/T_hot.
misconceptions: Computing efficiency as T_cold/T_hot
Thinking heat flows from cold to hot on its own

skills.name: Materials and stress
skills.intro_md: Stress is force over area and strain is change in length over original length. Young's modulus is the slope of the elastic part of the stress-strain curve.
misconceptions: Multiplying stress by area
Calling yielding a reversible change

skills.name: Fluids
skills.intro_md: Pressure grows with depth (p = ρgh). Bernoulli links faster flow to lower pressure, and an object floats when it is less dense than the fluid.
misconceptions: Thinking pressure depends on container shape
Believing heavier objects always sink

skills.name: Variables and types
skills.intro_md: A variable names a value; its type decides what the operators do. Assignment happens left to right, and the right side is evaluated first.
misconceptions: Expecting 3 / 2 to be integer division
Thinking a tuple assignment overwrites one value at a time

skills.name: Loops and ranges
skills.intro_md: range(start, stop) includes start and excludes stop. A while loop repeats while its condition holds, so the step size decides how many passes happen.
misconceptions: Including the stop value of a range
Miscounting the passes of a while loop with a step larger than 1

skills.name: Functions and scope
skills.intro_md: A function takes arguments, runs its body and returns a value (None if there is no return). Names created inside stay inside.
misconceptions: Assuming a function returns 0 by default
Expecting a local variable to exist outside its function

skills.name: Lists and slicing
skills.intro_md: Lists are indexed from 0. append adds to the end and a slice [a:b] keeps items from a up to but not including b.
misconceptions: Assuming lists are 1-indexed
Including the end index of a slice

skills.name: Recursion
skills.intro_md: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and stops at a base case. Trace it from the base case upward.
misconceptions: Writing the recursive call without shrinking the input
Tracing from the top instead of from the base case

skills.name: Big-O and efficiency
skills.intro_md: Big-O counts how work grows with input size: one loop is O(n), nested loops O(n²), halving each step O(log n).
misconceptions: Counting two sequential loops as O(n²)
Thinking a hash lookup is linear

skills.name: Whole-number arithmetic (practice)
skills.intro_md: Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division with whole numbers. Work from the place values; check a division by multiplying back.
misconceptions: Adding the digits of a product instead of multiplying
Borrowing without changing the next column

skills.name: Fraction practice
skills.intro_md: Rename fractions to a common denominator before adding or comparing them, and simplify by the greatest common factor.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators separately
Comparing fractions by denominator size alone

skills.name: Percent practice
skills.intro_md: Percent means per hundred. Find the part, the whole or the rate, and for a change divide by the *original* amount.
misconceptions: Subtracting a percent as a flat amount
Dividing the change by the new value

skills.name: Rate and proportion practice
skills.intro_md: Find the unit rate first, then scale it. In a proportion, cross-multiply or divide both sides by the same factor.
misconceptions: Scaling only one side of a proportion
Using the wrong base for a rate

skills.name: Area, perimeter and volume practice
skills.intro_md: Pick the formula that matches the shape: rectangle lw, triangle ½bh, circle πr², and volume = base area × height.
misconceptions: Using base × height for a triangle
Confusing radius and diameter

skills.name: Probability practice
skills.intro_md: Probability is favourable outcomes over total outcomes. Independent events multiply; 'not A' is 1 − P(A).
misconceptions: Adding probabilities for 'and'
Forgetting to subtract from 1 for 'not'

skills.name: Linear equations and slope (practice)
skills.intro_md: Undo operations in reverse order to isolate the variable, and remember slope = change in y over change in x.
misconceptions: Doing the same operation to only one side
Flipping the slope ratio

skills.name: SAT-style math practice
skills.intro_md: SAT math rewards clean setup: translate the sentence into an equation, then solve the equation you wrote.
misconceptions: Answering the wrong quantity
Forgetting to convert units

skills.name: ACT-style math practice
skills.intro_md: ACT math is fast: estimate first, then check the exact answer. Watch units and averages.
misconceptions: Averaging averages of unequal groups
Using the wrong time conversion

skills.name: AMC 8-style practice
skills.intro_md: AMC 8 problems are short but exact: count carefully, look for a pattern, and check the answer against the question asked.
misconceptions: Counting the same item twice
Solving for a quantity nobody asked for

skills.name: AMC 10-style practice
skills.intro_md: Choose counting tools by whether order matters, and use modular arithmetic for remainders.
misconceptions: Using combinations when order matters
Forgetting that 0 and 1 are special cases

skills.name: AMC 12-style practice
skills.intro_md: Logs turn products into sums, and sequences need the right formula before any numbers go in.
misconceptions: Treating a geometric sequence as arithmetic
Using log base 10 where base 2 is required

skills.name: AIME-style practice
skills.intro_md: AIME answers are integers: factor, count with inclusion–exclusion, and reduce every step to a whole number.
misconceptions: Counting divisors without the exponent rule
Adding counts without removing overlap

skills.name: USAMO-style practice
skills.intro_md: Olympiad algebra is about structure: symmetric expressions in sums and products, and careful case counts.
misconceptions: Squaring a sum without the cross term
Forgetting the negative case in an absolute value

skills.name: IMO-style practice
skills.intro_md: Use AM-GM for minimums with equality at equal terms, and angle/circle facts for geometry.
misconceptions: Applying AM-GM to non-positive numbers
Assuming equality away from the equal case

skills.name: Python output and semantics
skills.intro_md: Trace the code with real values, one line at a time. Watch integer division, slicing and 0-based indexing.
misconceptions: Assuming / is integer division
Forgetting that slices exclude the end index

skills.name: C++ output and semantics
skills.intro_md: C++ integer division truncates toward zero, and arrays are 0-based. Trace the loop bounds exactly.
misconceptions: Expecting integer division to produce a decimal
Using <= where the loop needs <

skills.name: Java output and semantics
skills.intro_md: In Java, int division truncates and + concatenates when either side is a String. Trace types as well as values.
misconceptions: Adding a String and an int numerically
Expecting int division to round

skills.name: SAT-style grammar and usage
skills.intro_md: Check the subject and verb agree, keep commas from joining two sentences, and make pronouns point at one clear noun.
misconceptions: Matching a verb to the nearest noun

questions.stem: 2x + y = 11 and y = x + 2

options.why: y must be x + 2.
2(5) + 1 = 11 works, but y ≠ x + 2.
2(2) + 7 = 11 works, but y ≠ x + 2.

hints: Substitute x + 2 for y in the first equation.

questions.stem: 2 burgers and 1 fries cost $13. 1 burger and 1 fries cost $8. What is the price of one burger?

options.why: Then fries would be $2 and 2(6) + 2 = $14, not $13.
Then fries would be $4 and 2(4) + 4 = $12.
That is the fries price, not the burger.

hints: Subtract the second order from the first.

questions.stem: Factor: x² + 7x + 12

options.why: Those multiply to 12 but add to 8, not 7.
Those add to 13.
Both signs would make the middle term −7x.

hints: Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.

questions.stem: Factor: x² − 5x + 6

options.why: That gives +5x in the middle.
That gives −7x in the middle.
That gives +x in the middle, not −5x.

hints: Two numbers multiply to +6 and add to −5.

questions.stem: Factor: x² − 9

options.why: That expands to x² − 6x + 9.
That expands to x² − 8x − 9.
A difference of two squares always factors.

hints: This is a difference of squares: a² − b².

questions.stem: Solve: x² + 2x − 15 = 0

options.why: Those come from (x − 5)(x + 3), which gives −2x in the middle.
Then the constant would be +15.
Then both the middle term and the constant have the wrong sign.

hints: Factor first: two numbers multiply to −15, add to +2.

questions.stem: A car speeds up from rest to 20 m/s with a constant acceleration of 4 m/s². How long does it take?

options.why: You multiplied 20 × 4 instead of dividing.
That is the acceleration value.
You added the numbers.

questions.stem: Starting from rest with a = 3 m/s², how far does an object travel in 4 s?

options.why: You used Δx = vt without the ½.
You forgot the ½ in ½at².
You used a/t instead of ½at².

questions.stem: An object has v₀ = 10 m/s, a = 2 m/s², and travels 24 m. What is its final speed?

options.why: That is v₀ + at for t = 1 s, not this distance.
That is v₀ + 2a·3, treating time as the distance.
That is v². You forgot the square root.

questions.stem: A car goes from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s, then travels at a constant 20 m/s for 10 s. What is the total distance?

options.why: That counts only the constant-speed part.
You used 20 m/s for the whole 15 s.
You treated the first 5 s as constant speed.

questions.stem: A 2 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². What net force acts on it?

options.why: You divided mass by acceleration.
You added the numbers.
You multiplied by 3 twice.

questions.stem: A 10 kg box is pushed with 40 N while 10 N of friction acts against it. What is its acceleration?

options.why: You used the applied force and ignored friction.
You added the forces instead of subtracting.
You used the friction force only.

questions.stem: A block slides down a frictionless 30° incline. What is its acceleration? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

options.why: That ignores the incline — only part of gravity acts along it.
That is g cos 30°, the perpendicular component.
You used g sin² 30°.

hints: Along the incline the component is g sin θ.

questions.stem: A 60 kg rider stands on a scale in an elevator and the scale reads 720 N. What is the elevator's acceleration? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

options.why: Then the scale would read 2mg.
The reading is above mg, so the acceleration is upward.
You used 720/60 as an acceleration without subtracting g.

hints: Normal force minus weight equals ma.

questions.stem: A 10 N force pushes a box 3 m in the direction of motion. How much work is done?

options.why: You divided force by distance.
You added force and distance.
The force and motion are parallel, so the work is not zero.

hints: W = Fd cos θ with θ = 0.

questions.stem: A 10 N force at 60° above the horizontal moves a box 3 m horizontally. How much work does the force do?

options.why: You ignored the angle.
You used sin 60°; the horizontal component uses cos.
Only a perpendicular force would do zero work.

hints: Only the component along the displacement does work.

questions.stem: A 5 kg box slides 4 m across a floor with μ = 0.2. What is the work done by friction? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

options.why: You used the mass alone instead of μmg.
Friction opposes motion, so its work is negative.
You used half the friction force.

hints: f = μN = μmg on a flat floor.

questions.stem: The net work done on a 2 kg block starting from rest is 25 J. What is its final speed?

options.why: You took the square root of 25/2.
That is K/m, not √(2K/m).
You used the work as a speed.

questions.stem: A force F = 4x (newtons, with x in metres) acts from x = 0 to x = 3 m. How much work is done?

options.why: You evaluated F at x = 3 and multiplied by 3.
You used 4x² instead of integrating.
You used the force at x = 1.5 only.

hints: Work is the area under F versus x.
The area is a triangle: ½ · base · height.

questions.stem: How much work is needed to stretch a spring (k = 200 N/m) by 0.2 m from its natural length?

options.why: You used kx without the ½ and squared wrongly.
You used ½kx² with kx doubled.
You used ½kx without squaring x.

questions.stem: A force increases linearly from 0 N to 12 N as an object moves 3 m. How much work is done?

options.why: You used the peak force for the whole distance (a rectangle).
You used half the distance.
You doubled the rectangle area.

hints: Linear increase means the graph is a triangle.

questions.stem: A spring with k = 200 N/m is already stretched 0.2 m. How much extra work is needed to stretch it to 0.4 m?

options.why: That is the work to reach 0.2 m, not the extra.
That is ½k(0.4)² alone, which double-counts the first stretch.
You used ½k(0.4)² with k doubled.

hints: Use the difference of elastic energies.

questions.stem: The net work done on a cart is 50 J. What is its change in kinetic energy?

options.why: You halved it; the theorem is an equality.
Positive net work increases kinetic energy.
The theorem does not need the mass.

questions.stem: A block slides 2 m down a frictionless 30° incline from rest. What is its speed at the bottom? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

options.why: You dropped the factor of 2 under the root.
That is g, not the speed.
You used the full 2 m as the height.

questions.stem: A 2 kg block slides 2 m down a 30° incline. Gravity would add 19.6 J of kinetic energy, but friction removes 5 J. What is the final speed?

options.why: That ignores friction.
You subtracted 5 J twice.
You used K/m instead of 2K/m.

questions.stem: A motor does 300 J of work in 5 s. What is its average power?

options.why: You multiplied work by time.
You used the work as the power.
You divided time by work.

questions.stem: A 3 kg ball moves at 4 m/s. What is its momentum?

options.why: You added mass and speed.
You divided mass by speed.
You doubled the product.

questions.stem: A 20 N force acts for 0.5 s. What impulse does it deliver?

options.why: You divided by 0.5 instead of multiplying.
You divided force by time.
You halved the force instead of multiplying by time.

questions.stem: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s hits a 4 kg cart at rest and they stick together. What is their common speed?

options.why: You divided by the 4 kg cart only.
You forgot to add the masses.
You used 2 × 3 / 12.

hints: Momentum is conserved in the collision.
p = 6 kg·m/s before; total mass 6 kg after.

questions.stem: A 4 kg ball moving at 5 m/s elastically strikes an identical ball at rest. What happens?

options.t: The first stops and the second moves at 5 m/s

options.why: That is the perfectly inelastic outcome.

options.t: The first continues at 5 m/s and the second stays still
options.why: That would violate momentum conservation.
There is no reason for a reversal in a head-on elastic hit.

hints: For equal masses in a 1-D elastic collision, the velocities exchange.
Momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved.

questions.stem: If 2x + 3 = 11, what is x?

options.why: You subtracted 3 from 11 and stopped.
You divided 11 by 2 before subtracting.
You added 3 instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: If 3(x − 2) = 15, what is x?

options.why: You divided by 3 and stopped.
You distributed incorrectly.
You added 2 twice.

hints: Divide both sides by 3 first, or distribute.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line through (0, 3) and (4, 11)?

options.why: That is only the change in y.
You inverted the ratio.
That is the y-intercept.

questions.stem: If 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2, what is x?

options.why: That is y, not x.
That is x + 2.
That is 9/2 from adding the equations incorrectly.

hints: Adding the two equations eliminates y.

questions.stem: What is 15% of 80?

options.why: That is the percentage itself.
That is 10% of 80.
You moved the decimal one place too far.

questions.stem: A $40 item is 25% off. What is the sale price?

options.why: That is the discount, not the price.
That is a 12.5% discount.
That is a 20% discount.

questions.stem: A value increases from 50 to 65. What is the percent increase?

options.why: That is the absolute change, not the percent.
You divided by the new value (15/65).
That is the new value as a percent of the old.

questions.stem: A $100 item is discounted 20%, then the reduced price is discounted another 10%. What is the final price?

options.why: You added the discounts (30% off). They compound.
You applied 10% to the original price.
You applied only the second discount.

questions.stem: Two numbers are in the ratio 3:5 and add to 40. What is the larger number?

options.why: That is the smaller number.
That comes from splitting 40 into 5:8.
That is one part, not the larger share.

questions.stem: 4 identical items cost $10. What is the cost per item?

options.why: You divided the wrong way.
You moved the decimal too far.
You halved the price twice.

hints: Unit rate = total cost ÷ number of items.

questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 cups of sugar. How much flour is needed for 6 cups of sugar?

options.why: You added 1 instead of scaling.
You matched sugar to flour 1:1.
You doubled the sugar ratio incorrectly.

questions.stem: A car travels 120 miles in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed?

options.why: You divided by 2 hours instead of 2.5.
You multiplied instead of dividing.
You rounded the time to 2.4 hours.

questions.stem: What is the area of a rectangle with sides 6 and 9?

options.why: That is the perimeter.
That is the sum of the sides.
You used 2 × 6 × 9.

hints: Area of a rectangle = length × width.

questions.stem: What is the area of a triangle with base 8 and height 5?

options.why: You forgot the ½.
You added the numbers.
You used ½(8 + 5) × 4.

questions.stem: What is the area of a circle with radius 3?

options.why: You used the radius instead of the square.
That is the circumference.
You squared the diameter.

questions.stem: A square has side 4, and a semicircle of radius 2 sits on one of its sides. What is the total area?

options.why: You used a full circle.
You used ½πr with r = 2.
You doubled the square.

hints: Square area plus half of a circle of radius 2.

questions.stem: If f(x) = 2x + 1, what is f(3)?

options.why: You forgot the +1.
You added the input to the function.
You used 2 × 3 + 3.

questions.stem: If f(x) = x² − 4, what is f(−3)?

options.why: You squared −3 as −9; squaring a negative gives a positive.
You used +9 and added 4.
You forgot to subtract 4.

questions.stem: If g(x) = 3x − 2 and g(x) = 10, what is x?

options.why: You did 3(10) − 2.
You divided 10 by 2 incorrectly.

questions.stem: If f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, what is f(g(2))?

options.why: You did g(f(2)).
You used g(2) as the answer.
You multiplied instead of substituting.

hints: Work from the inside out: g(2) first.

questions.stem: Which organelle is the main site of ATP production in a eukaryotic cell?

options.why: Ribosomes build proteins; they do not generate the cell's ATP supply.
The Golgi packages and ships proteins — it consumes ATP rather than making it.
Lysosomes digest material; they are not the cell's power plant.

hints: Which organelle has folded inner membranes called cristae?
The same one uses the electron transport chain.
steps: Mitochondria run oxidative phosphorylation on their inner membrane.
That is where most ATP is made.

questions.stem: A cell that secretes large amounts of protein hormones would contain an unusually large amount of which structure?

options.why: Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies; secreted proteins are built on the rough ER.
Lysosomes break material down; they do not build proteins for export.
Peroxisomes handle fatty acids and peroxide, not protein synthesis for secretion.

hints: Secreted proteins are translated by ribosomes bound to a membrane.
steps: Ribosomes on the rough ER translate the protein into the ER lumen.
The Golgi then packages it for secretion.

questions.stem: A plant cell and an animal cell are both placed in distilled water. Which statement best explains why only the animal cell bursts?

options.t: The plant cell wall resists expansion, so the cell becomes turgid instead of bursting.
The plant cell has no membrane, so water cannot enter it.
options.why: Every cell has a plasma membrane; the wall is additional.

options.t: The plant cell actively pumps all water back out.
options.why: Water still enters by osmosis; the wall is what prevents bursting.

options.t: The plant cell contains no solutes, so osmosis stops.
options.why: Plant cells contain many solutes, which is why water enters at all.

hints: Water moves toward the side with more solute.
What extra layer does a plant cell have outside its membrane?
steps: Osmosis pulls water into both cells.
The rigid wall pushes back, so pressure rises without rupture.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the function of the Golgi apparatus. Which process is most directly affected?

options.t: Modifying and packaging proteins for transport out of the cell
Transcribing DNA into mRNA in the nucleus
options.why: Transcription happens in the nucleus and does not require the Golgi.

options.t: Generating a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.why: That is the mitochondrion's job.
Replication occurs in the nucleus during S phase.

hints: Think about what happens to a protein after the rough ER.
The Golgi is the cell's sorting and shipping centre.
steps: Proteins leave the ER and enter the Golgi.
Without the Golgi they are not modified, sorted or shipped.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 18 g of water? (Molar mass of H₂O = 18 g/mol)

options.why: That would be 18 g/mol × 18, treating grams as moles.
You divided 18 by 36; the molar mass is 18 g/mol.
You multiplied grams by the molar mass instead of dividing.

questions.stem: Which bond forms when one atom transfers electrons to another?

options.why: Covalent bonds share electrons; transfer is ionic.
Hydrogen bonds are attractions between molecules, not electron transfer.
Metallic bonding pools electrons across a lattice rather than transferring them to one atom.

hints: Transfer means one atom gains electrons and the other loses them.
Which bond is between a metal and a nonmetal?
steps: A metal loses electrons and becomes a cation.
A nonmetal gains them and becomes an anion — an ionic bond.

questions.stem: How many formula units are in 0.50 mol of NaCl? (Use 6.0 × 10²³ per mole.)

options.why: That is one full mole; you have half a mole.
You multiplied by 2 instead of by 0.5.
The exponent is off by ten — check 0.5 × 6.0.

questions.stem: Which 1-mole sample contains the greatest number of atoms?

options.why: One mole of water has 3 mol of atoms (2 H + 1 O).
One mole of CO₂ has 3 mol of atoms, fewer than CH₄'s 5.
One mole of O₂ has only 2 mol of atoms.

hints: Count the atoms in one formula unit.
CH₄ has one carbon and four hydrogens.
steps: So 1 mol CH₄ holds 5 mol of atoms, the largest of the four.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

options.t: The experiment failed; however, the data were still useful.
The experiment failed, however, the data were still useful.
options.why: Two complete sentences joined by a comma is a comma splice. Use a semicolon or a period.

options.t: The experiment failed however the data were still useful.
options.why: A conjunctive adverb between two complete sentences needs punctuation before it.

options.t: The experiment failed, however; the data were still useful.
options.why: The semicolon belongs before 'however', not after it.

hints: 'The experiment failed' and 'the data were still useful' are both complete sentences.
A conjunctive adverb like 'however' needs a semicolon before it.
steps: Two independent clauses need a semicolon, period or comma + conjunction.

questions.stem: Which choice fixes the comma splice: 'The samples were stored at −20 °C, they remained stable for a year.'

options.t: The samples were stored at −20 °C; they remained stable for a year.
The samples were stored at −20 °C, they remained stable for a year, too.
options.why: Adding a word does not remove the splice — two complete sentences still meet at a comma.

options.t: The samples were stored at −20 °C they remained stable for a year.
options.why: Removing the comma leaves a run-on with no boundary at all.

options.t: The samples were stored, at −20 °C, they remained stable for a year.
options.why: A comma after 'stored' splits a verb from its object and keeps the splice.

hints: Count the subjects and verbs on each side.
Both halves could stand alone as sentences.
steps: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone.
Replace the comma with a semicolon.

questions.stem: Which sentence needs a comma after its opening phrase?

options.t: After the centrifuge stopped the technician removed the tubes.
The technician removed the tubes after the centrifuge stopped.
options.why: Nothing opens the sentence here, so no comma is needed.

options.t: The tubes that were removed had already been labelled.
options.why: This begins with the subject, not an introductory phrase.

options.t: Removing the tubes took longer than expected.
options.why: A gerund phrase acting as the subject takes no comma.

hints: Look for a phrase before the main subject.
In the first option, where does the introductory phrase end?
steps: 'After the centrifuge stopped' is an introductory clause.
It takes a comma before 'the technician'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly?

options.t: Three trials were run; each used a fresh sample.
Three trials were run; and each used a fresh sample.
options.why: Do not put a semicolon before a coordinating conjunction joining two clauses.

options.t: Three trials were run; using a fresh sample each time.
options.why: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; the second part is a fragment.

options.t: Three trials; were run using a fresh sample each time.
options.why: The semicolon splits the subject from its verb.

hints: A semicolon joins two complete sentences.
Check whether both sides could stand alone.
steps: 'Three trials were run' and 'each used a fresh sample' are both complete.

questions.stem: Passage: 'The lab's oldest freezer was finally retired. Its replacement arrived on Tuesday, and by Thursday every sample had been transferred.' What can be inferred?

options.t: The samples needed to stay frozen during the move.
The old freezer was repaired instead of replaced.
options.why: The passage says it was retired and a replacement arrived.

options.t: The samples were destroyed in the transfer.
options.why: Nothing suggests loss; the transfer was completed.

options.t: The new freezer arrived after Thursday.
options.why: It arrived on Tuesday, before the transfer.

hints: Why move samples quickly from one freezer to another?
What happens to samples if they warm up?
steps: Samples in a freezer are temperature-sensitive.
A fast transfer keeps them frozen.

questions.stem: Passage: 'Although the second draft was shorter, reviewers requested even more cuts before publication.' What does this suggest about the reviewers?

options.t: They thought the piece still contained unnecessary material.
They wanted the author to add supporting detail.
options.why: They asked for cuts, which removes material.

options.t: They had not read the second draft.
options.why: They comment on the second draft specifically.
The passage never compares drafts by preference, only by length.

hints: What does asking for 'more cuts' mean?
How does that relate to the draft already being shorter?
steps: Asking for more cuts implies material still to remove.

questions.stem: Passage: 'The museum extended its hours for the exhibition's final week. Attendance that week was triple the monthly average.' What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.t: Longer hours contributed to the higher attendance.
The exhibition was unpopular for most of the month.
options.why: We only know the final week's spike, not overall popularity.

options.t: The museum lost money that week.
options.why: Higher attendance says nothing about costs or revenue.

options.t: Attendance is always triple in the last week of a show.
options.why: The passage gives no such general pattern — this one moved its hours.

hints: Which explanation links the change to the attendance?
steps: The only change mentioned is the extended hours.
So the increase is best explained by the hours.

questions.stem: Passage: 'The recipe calls for room-temperature eggs, but the note in the margin warns that cold eggs will curdle the batter.' What does the margin note do?

options.t: It explains why the temperature instruction matters.

options.why: It supports the instruction by giving a reason.

options.t: It suggests replacing eggs with another ingredient.
options.why: No substitute is mentioned.

options.t: It describes how to warm the eggs.
options.why: No warming method is given.

hints: What is the note attached to?
Does it agree with the instruction or explain it?
steps: The instruction says use room-temperature eggs.
The note supplies the consequence of ignoring it.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion was ______: two independent teams reached it without sharing data.

options.why: 'Tentative' means uncertain, but independent agreement strengthens a conclusion.
Redundant means unnecessary repetition, not independent confirmation.
Haste is about speed, and the sentence is about agreement.

hints: Does that make the finding stronger or weaker?
steps: Independent confirmation makes a result more reliable.

questions.stem: Although the editor praised the essay's argument, she found its prose ______ and asked for a rewrite.

options.why: Concise prose is compact; a rewrite request after praise suggests a problem, not brevity.
Polished prose would not prompt a rewrite.
Candour means honesty, which is not a fault to fix.

hints: The 'although' signals a contrast with praise.
The rewrite request suggests the writing is hard to follow.
steps: Contrast: good argument, problem with prose.
'Convoluted' means tangled and hard to follow.

questions.stem: The city's new bus lanes had a ______ effect: average commute times fell by eleven minutes within a month.

options.why: An eleven-minute drop is not negligible.
Speculative describes something unproven, but the effect was measured.
The passage gives no evidence the result was a surprise.

hints: Is an eleven-minute drop large or small?

questions.stem: Rather than ______ the criticism, the author revised the chapter and thanked the reviewer in the next edition.

options.why: Soliciting criticism means asking for it, which does not fit 'rather than'.
The author responded after the criticism, not in advance.
Endorsing criticism does not contrast with revising.

hints: 'Rather than' sets up a contrast with revising.
Which verb names the opposite response to criticism?
steps: The contrast is refusing the criticism versus acting on it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English? 'The survey was sent to 400 households ______ only 120 were returned.'

options.why: A comma alone between two complete sentences is a comma splice.
A colon must follow an independent clause and introduce what follows; here it separates two full sentences.
Without punctuation the two sentences run together.

hints: Two complete sentences need a semicolon, period or comma + conjunction.
steps: 'The survey was sent to 400 households' is complete.
'Only 120 were returned' is complete too — use a semicolon.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English? 'Marie Tharp, ______ mapped the ocean floor, changed how geologists understood plate tectonics.'

options.why: This closes the non-essential phrase early and leaves 'mapped the ocean floor' dangling.
The words are out of order.
'Whom' would be the object, but this person is the subject of 'mapped'.

hints: The phrase between the commas describes Tharp.
steps: The appositive is 'a cartographer who mapped the ocean floor'.
Only the first choice keeps it intact.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English? 'The museum's collection includes works by Rivera, Kahlo, and Siqueiros ______ none of the three is on display this month.'

options.why: A comma would splice two complete sentences.
A semicolon plus a conjunction is not a standard boundary.
A colon after a list does not introduce a contrasting full sentence well here; the second sentence stands on its own.

hints: Both sides of the gap are complete sentences.
steps: The first sentence lists artists; the second is a new statement.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English? 'Because the samples were kept in the dark ______ the algae lost their colour.'

options.why: A semicolon cannot follow a dependent clause introduced by 'because'.
A colon needs a complete clause before it; 'Because the samples were kept in the dark' is not one.
The dependent clause needs a comma before the main clause.

hints: What punctuation closes an introductory dependent clause?
steps: Introductory dependent clause + comma + main clause.

questions.stem: A printer produces 45 pages in 3 minutes. At the same rate, how many pages does it produce in 8 minutes?

options.why: That is 45 × 2 minutes, but you need 8 minutes.
That would be 9 minutes of printing.
That is the pages-per-minute rate, not an 8-minute total.

hints: Find the rate per minute first.

questions.stem: A jacket originally priced at $80 is discounted 25%, then an additional 10% is taken off the sale price. What is the final price?

options.why: That subtracts 35% at once; successive discounts multiply, they do not add.
That applies only the 25% and then subtracts $4.
That applies only the first discount.

hints: Apply the discounts one after the other.

questions.stem: A car travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed in miles per hour?

options.why: That is 150 ÷ 2, ignoring the extra half hour.
You multiplied distance by time.
Check the division: 150 ÷ 2.5.

questions.stem: A solution is 15% acid. How many litres of pure acid are in 240 litres of the solution?

options.why: That is the percentage, not the amount.
That is 10% of 240.
Decimal point slipped: 0.15 × 240 = 36.

hints: Convert the percent to a decimal.

questions.stem: The table records three trials of a filter. What is the flow rate, in mL per second?

options.why: That inverts the ratio: you divided seconds by millilitres.
That is the change between trials, not the rate within a trial.
That is the time, not the rate.

hints: Use any row: 10 mL in 20 s.
steps: Every row gives the same rate.

questions.stem: What is the smallest positive integer x with x ≡ 3 (mod 4) and x ≡ 5 (mod 7)?
How many trailing zeros does 20! have?

options.why: That counts only the factor 100 inside 20!.
That counts the multiples of 5 but stops one short.
That counts 5, 10, 15, 20 and then adds an extra.

hints: Each trailing zero needs a factor of 10 = 2 × 5.

questions.stem: What is 2¹⁰ mod 1000?

options.why: That subtracts 900 instead of 1000.
That is 2⁹, one power short.
That is 2¹⁰ itself, not its remainder mod 1000.

hints: 2¹⁰ = 1024, then subtract the largest multiple of 1000.

questions.stem: How many primes are there between 90 and 100?

options.why: 91 = 7 × 13 and 93 = 3 × 31 are not prime.
97 is prime, so the count is not zero.
99 = 9 × 11, so it is not prime.

hints: Primes are not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7.

questions.stem: What is the largest prime factor of 210?

options.why: 11 does not divide 210.
5 is a factor, but 7 is larger.
3 is a factor, but smaller than 7.

questions.stem: For how many integers n from 1 to 30 is n² − 1 divisible by 8?

options.why: That counts only multiples of 4.
That counts even n, but even n give n² − 1 odd.
n² − 1 is not divisible by 8 for every n.

hints: n² − 1 = (n − 1)(n + 1), a product of two numbers two apart.
Check odd and even n separately.
steps: For odd n, n − 1 and n + 1 are consecutive even numbers, so one is divisible by 4.

questions.stem: In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles are…

options.why: That is true for a parallelogram, not for every cyclic quadrilateral.
Complementary angles add to 90°, which would force a right angle pair.
Only a rectangle inscribed in a circle has all right angles.

hints: Opposite angles subtend arcs that add to the whole circle.
steps: Together the two arcs are 360°, so the angles add to 180°.

questions.stem: What is the area of an equilateral triangle with side 6?

options.why: That uses ½ × 6 × 6√3, which double counts the height.
That is the square of the side.
That uses side 4√3 in the area formula.

questions.stem: From a point 10 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 6, a tangent is drawn. How long is the tangent segment?

options.why: That subtracts the radius from the distance instead of using Pythagoras.
That is the radius.
That is the distance to the centre.

hints: The radius meets the tangent at a right angle.

questions.stem: What is 15% of 60?

options.why: That is 10% of 60.
That is 20% of 60.
That copies the percent instead of applying it.

questions.stem: How many minutes are there from 2:45 to 3:20?

options.why: That subtracts 20 from 45 and ignores the hour change.
That adds the minutes instead of finding the gap.
That counts a full hour and subtracts the wrong way.

questions.stem: The average of five numbers is 12. What is their sum?

options.why: That is the average of the first ten integers, not this sum.
That adds the count to the average.
That is the average itself.

questions.stem: A shirt costs $24 after a 20% discount. What was the original price?

options.why: That adds 20% of the sale price, which is not the same base.
That is a 25% discount from $32.
That adds the 20 dollars of discount twice.

hints: The sale price is 80% of the original.

questions.stem: How many two-digit positive integers contain the digit 7?

options.why: That counts only the 70s and misses 17, 27, ….
That counts 77 twice.
That includes 07, which is not a two-digit number.

hints: Count the 70s, then the numbers ending in 7.
steps: 10 numbers in the 70s, plus 8 more ending in 7 outside the 70s (17, 27, 37, 47, 57, 67, 87, 97).

questions.stem: How many three-digit numbers can be made using only odd digits, if repeats are allowed?

options.why: That uses 4 digits per position.
That is the count without repeats.
That uses 5 choices for two positions and 4 for the third.

hints: Each of the three positions has 5 choices.

questions.stem: The product of three consecutive integers is 120. What is the largest of the three?

options.why: 8 × 9 × 10 is much more than 120.
4 × 5 × 6 = 120, and 5 is the middle number, not the largest.
6 × 7 × 8 is far more than 120.

hints: The cube root of 120 is about 5, so the middle number is near 5.

questions.stem: How many zeros are at the end of 15!?

options.why: That is the count for 20!.
That counts only the number 10 itself.
That counts only multiples of 10.

steps: 5, 10 and 15 each bring a factor of 5, and there are plenty of 2s.

questions.stem: A cube has edges of length 3 cm. What is its total surface area?

options.why: That is the volume, 3³.
That counts four faces instead of six.
That is 2 × 3², only two faces.

questions.stem: What is the units digit of 7²⁵?

options.why: That is the units digit when the exponent is a multiple of 4.
That is 7³'s units digit.
That is 7²'s units digit.

hints: The units digits of powers of 7 repeat 7, 9, 3, 1.
steps: 25 = 4 × 6 + 1, so the pattern lands on its first entry.

questions.stem: A rectangle is 7 cm by 4 cm. What is the square of its diagonal?

options.why: That is the area, not the diagonal.
That adds the sides and then adds 11 again.
That adds the sides instead of squaring them.

options.why: That is the area.
That is three sides of length 8.
That is twice the side, not four times it.

options.why: That makes the angles add to 150°.
That makes the angles add to 300°.
That makes the angles add to 200°.

questions.stem: How many edges does a cube have?

options.why: That is the number of faces.
That is the number of vertices.
That counts each edge twice, once per face.

hints: Count the edges around the top, the bottom, and the vertical ones.

options.why: That is the area.
That doubles the diameter.
That uses the radius instead of the diameter.

options.why: That is 8 × 7 × 6, which counts orderings.
That is 8³.
That is 8 × 3, which overcounts and ignores order.

hints: Order does not matter, so this is a combination.

questions.stem: How many three-digit positive integers are even?

options.why: That assumes half of 1000, including one- and two-digit numbers.
That is the count of all three-digit numbers.
That uses 4 hundreds digits and 100 endings.

hints: Three-digit numbers run from 100 to 999: 900 of them.

questions.stem: How many subsets does a 5-element set have?

options.why: That is 5², treating choices as dependent.
That is the count for a 4-element set.
That counts only pairs.

hints: Each element is either in or out.

options.why: That counts only half of the six winning pairs.
That counts 7 pairs instead of 6.
That is 4/36, the chance of a sum of 5.

hints: List the pairs that sum to 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4) and reverses.
There are 6 winning pairs out of 36.

Plants combine sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant takes up water from the soil?

options.why: Leaves lose water and make food; they do not absorb soil water.
Flowers are for reproduction.
Seeds store food for a new plant.

hints: Root hairs absorb water and minerals.
steps: Roots take up water from the soil.

questions.stem: Fungi get their energy by…

options.why: Fungi have no chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise.
Most fungi do not hunt.
Fungi are not filter feeders.

questions.stem: An animal that eats only plants is a…

options.why: Omnivores eat both plants and animals.
Decomposers break down dead matter.
Carnivores eat other animals.

questions.stem: Which of these is a state of matter?

options.why: Sound is a wave travelling through matter.
Energy is not a state of matter.
Force is an interaction, not a form of matter.

hints: Matter comes in solid, liquid and gas.
Which option names one of them?
steps: Solid is a state of matter.

questions.stem: Water freezes into ice at…

options.why: That is the boiling point of water.
That is the freezing point in degrees Fahrenheit, not Celsius.
That is far below water's freezing point.

hints: The Celsius scale puts freezing at zero.

Salt is not magnetic.
Freezing separates ice from salt water only partly, and leaves brine behind.

Remove the water and the salt stays behind.
steps: That is how sea salt is made.

questions.stem: In a chemical change…

options.why: Chemical reactions absorb or release energy.
Mass is conserved in a chemical change.
Shape changes are physical changes.

hints: Look for a new substance with new properties.
Burning, rusting and baking are examples.
steps: A chemical change produces new substances.
The atoms are rearranged, not destroyed.

questions.stem: Force is measured in…

options.why: Joules measure energy.
Watts measure power.
Metres measure length.

hints: The unit is named after the scientist who wrote the laws of motion.

steps: No net force means no change in motion.

options.why: That divides by 10 twice.
The mass is on Earth, so gravity acts on it.
That uses the mass as the weight.

They act everywhere, including on the ground.

unequal, with the bigger object winning

questions.stem: Earth orbits…

options.why: Mars is a separate planet in its own orbit.
Orbiting itself is not a thing.
The Moon orbits Earth, not the other way round.

hints: Which body is at the centre of our solar system?
The star we see in the daytime sky.
steps: Earth orbits the Sun once a year.

questions.stem: Day and night are caused by…

options.why: The orbit causes the year and the seasons, not day and night.
That only happens during a solar eclipse.
The Sun does not orbit Earth.

steps: Rotation brings each side into sunlight and then into shadow.

options.why: The distance change is small and not the cause.

options.t: the Sun gets hotter in summer
options.why: The Sun's output does not change with our seasons.

questions.stem: The Moon's phases repeat about every…

That is Earth's orbit around the Sun.

questions.stem: The energy stored in food is…

Digestion does not split atoms.
Sound is a wave, not how food stores energy.

questions.stem: A moving ball has…

options.why: A moving object has kinetic energy.
Motion is energy.
A rolling ball is not a circuit.

steps: The ball has kinetic energy, ½mv².

questions.stem: Energy cannot be…

options.why: Batteries and food store energy.
Energy is transferred all the time.
Energy changes form constantly.

hints: The law of conservation of energy.
steps: Energy is conserved: it moves and changes form but is not created or destroyed.

questions.stem: A roller coaster at the top of a hill has mostly…

Sound is a by-product, not the main store.
The car is not burning fuel at the top.

As it drops, that store becomes kinetic.
steps: High up means large gravitational potential energy.

questions.stem: Sound travels as…

Sound moves energy, not matter, across the room.
Light and sound are different.

hints: Sound is a vibration travelling through a medium.

Volume is amplitude, not frequency.

Sound is longitudinal in water too.
